title: The Last Typewriter
premise: In the final months of the Great War, Elodie Ravensworth drives for imprisoned suffragist Verity Ashcombe, secretly reading and copying every letter that passes through her hands on a battered typewriter. When a shell-shocked soldier named Tobias Crane arrives bearing letters in Verity's handwriting — written after her official death in custody — Elodie realizes the state has buried a living woman to erase a scandal. Racing censors, informants, and the approaching armistice, Elodie and Tobias smuggle the correspondence to a sympathetic journalist, getting the truth notarized and printed hours before the victors' historians can seal the record. Verity survives to see her name restored, but Elodie must choose between the invisible life she trusted and a public testimony that costs her her anonymity forever.
about_author: Tamsin Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated wartime correspondence in regional record offices. She writes historical fiction about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Introduces her routine driving for Verity Ashcombe under house arrest, reading letters by lamplight before delivery and typing copies into a hidden folio. Establishes her creed: carry only what fits in two hands. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: The Prisoner's Penmanship
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A stranger, Tobias Crane, intercepts her route with letters dated weeks after Verity's reported death from pneumonia in Holloway's infirmary. The handwriting is unmistakable — Elodie has copied it a hundred times. Beat: vertigo; the ground of her careful world tilts.

chapters.title: A Corpse Who Writes
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. He explains he was a hospital orderly who smuggled out letters from a woman registered under a false name, 'Mrs. Grey,' before his transfer to the front. He came back from France with shrapnel and a promise. Beat: desperate hope seeking a witness.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She verifies the letters against her own typewritten archive — matching phrases, a recurring ink blot, the private shorthand she alone would recognize. Verity lives. Beat: elation curdling into fear of what proving it will cost.

chapters.title: Orders Come at Dusk
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Government men arrive to collect Verity's effects for 'archival destruction' ahead of an armistice amnesty scrubbing embarrassing cases. Elodie hides her folio inside a spare tire well. Beat: first open confrontation with the machinery of erasure.

chapters.title: The Journalist Who Owes Nobody
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. They approach Augustus Pell, a disgraced war correspondent drinking in a Soho pub, who once promised to print truth and then printed casualty figures instead. He refuses — until Elodie reads him one letter aloud. Beat: cynicism cracked by a single human sentence.

chapters.title: Notarized in a Back Room
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A sympathetic solicitor, Miss Okonkwo's chambers, swears affidavits authenticating the handwriting against Elodie's archive. The truth is now 'on the record' — but a record no one reads. Beat: fragile triumph, the sense of holding water in cupped hands.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading Our Mail
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. Evidence surfaces that their correspondence is being intercepted: a copied letter returned with a censor's stamp, a tail outside the garage. Elodie's creed of invisibility has failed. Beat: paranoia tightening like a wire.

chapters.title: Loyalty Has Two Faces
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Her sister Cressida, a civil servant, warns Elodie she's been named in a file and begs her to burn everything. Family loyalty versus truth. Elodie lies to her sister's face for the first time. Beat: guilt as a physical ache.

chapters.title: Holloway, Revisited
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. They trace 'Mrs. Grey' through a discharged matron who confirms a woman was moved out the night before her death certificate was signed — alive, sedated, driven north. Beat: horror at how orderly the lie was.

chapters.title: The House in Northumberland
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Following the trail, they find the estate where Verity is held under another alias, guarded thinly because no one believes anyone is looking. Elodie sees her employer through a window, thinner, still writing. Beat: longing at a distance, refusal to leave empty-handed.

chapters.title: A Letter That Must Not Arrive
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie gets a note to Verity through a kitchen maid; the reply, in that unmistakable hand, says: do not come for me, finish the record first. Verity chooses truth over rescue. Beat: Elodie's obedience to her own principles tested against love.

chapters.title: Cressida's Choice
chapters.summary: Cressida's POV (first departure). Torn between career and conscience, Cressida discovers the file naming Elodie includes orders for detention after the armistice celebrations. She copies a page and leaves it anonymously. Beat: loyalty realigning toward truth.

chapters.title: Pell's Deadline
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. Pell secures column inches in a Manchester paper for the day before the expected armistice — one chance, no corrections. But printing requires the original letters, which means transporting them through a city preparing to erupt in celebration or riot. Beat: the clock becomes audible.

chapters.title: The Informant in the Garage
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The mechanic who helped hide the folio is arrested; his confession names a 'woman driver.' Elodie must move the archive tonight or lose it. She types a final duplicate set and scatters decoys. Beat: sacrifice of her last safe place.

chapters.title: Armistice Eve
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Bells begin ringing prematurely; crowds flood the streets. In the chaos, Elodie and Tobias transport the letters in the ambulance-style car, stopped twice by police, talked through both checkpoints by nerve and forged papers. Beat: terror transfigured into purpose.

chapters.title: Set in Type
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. At the Manchester print works overnight, compositors set the story while Pell argues with the owner over legal risk. The affidavits hold. Dawn brings the first proofs. Beat: the sacred, mechanical clatter of truth becoming public.

chapters.title: The Morning Edition
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs. The story breaks: 'THE WOMAN THE STATE BURIED.' Crowds read aloud on street corners; questions are asked in Parliament within hours; the Home Office cannot unprint it. Beat: catharsis — the record now belongs to everyone.

chapters.title: They Come for Elodie
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Detained anyway, Elodie faces an official who offers quiet release in exchange for surrendering her archive and silence. She refuses, citing the notarized copies already beyond reach. Beat: the climax of principle — justice claimed outside the law's permission.

chapters.title: Verity Walks Out
chapters.summary: Verity's POV (second departure). Public pressure forces her release; she walks past reporters straight to the waiting car — Elodie's car. Their reunion is wordless, then fierce. Beat: belonging found, not granted.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At the inquiry, Elodie testifies publicly, surrendering anonymity forever, her typed archive entered as evidence. Cressida sits in the gallery. The officials responsible resign quietly; the women they erased are named. Beat: cost accepted, dignity kept.

chapters.title: The Last Typewriter
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, epilogue. Years later, Elodie keeps the old machine on a desk by a window, teaching young women to type their own records. Verity writes; Elodie no longer needs to read in secret. Final line: some things, once carried, are never put down. Beat: peace earned, legacy begun.
